basis: creation, animal rule, slavery after sin
note: Augustine argues that the created order gives humans rule over irrational creatures, while human slavery is bound to sin; this Christian reading separates animal dominion from a natural right to own persons.

basis: Human creation directed toward God
note: The commentary treats being created as the ground of belonging to God; Augustine opens by interpreting human creation as oriented toward God and rest in God, adding an account of the human longing that accompanies creaturely dependence.

basis: master and slave hope in the same God
note: The Didache forbids bitter commands to male or female slaves because both slave and master hope in the same God; it applies common divine lordship to household conduct.

ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4
basis: buying humans made in God's image
note: Gregory's homily on Ecclesiastes 2:7 attacks the purchase of human beings by appealing to their divine image and created freedom, a pointed patristic challenge to calling a person property.

basis: slaves serve for God's glory and better freedom
note: Ignatius tells enslaved Christians to serve more diligently for God's glory so that they may receive a better freedom from God, preserving the tension between social servitude and divine freedom.

basis: Believers are not their own
note: The commentary says the human servant belongs to an owner; Paul tells the Corinthians they are not their own because they were bought at a price, giving a direct ownership formulation.

basis: bought with a price and glorify God
note: Believers are said to have been bought at a price and therefore to glorify God bodily, joining ownership language to a lived act of worship.

basis: A free person called in Christ is Christ's slave
note: The commentary says free and enslaved people alike are God's servants; Paul calls the free person who is called by the Lord Christ's slave, making freedom and divine belonging coexist.

basis: slave as Lord's freedperson, free as Christ's slave
note: Paul reverses ordinary social labels: the enslaved called in the Lord is free, while the free person is Christ's slave; it sharply reframes the commentary's fixed owner-slave status.

basis: Bought with a price, not slaves of humans
note: The commentary places divine ownership above the human master's claim; Paul says believers were bought with a price and must not become slaves of humans, explicitly limiting human ownership.

basis: bought at a price; do not become human slaves
note: Because believers were bought at a price, Paul warns them not to become slaves of humans; divine purchase becomes an argument against human mastery.

basis: A free speaker makes himself a slave to others
note: The commentary says the servant's status is not initiated by choice because it follows creation; Paul says that though free he made himself a slave to all, offering a contrasting voluntary form of service for others.

basis: Free people remain God's servants
note: The commentary says human freedom does not cancel being God's servant; Peter tells believers to live as free people while remaining God's servants, holding both statuses together.

basis: free people as slaves of God
note: Believers are to live as free people while also as God's slaves; the deliberate pairing gives a Christian reversal of the commentary's ordinary contrast between freedom and owned status.

basis: Slaves owe honor to human masters
note: The commentary's B006 gloss describes someone honored as if worshipped; Timothy tells enslaved believers to regard their masters as worthy of honor, adding a household rule that distinguishes human honor from divine worship.

basis: only Sovereign, King of kings, Lord of lords
note: The doxology calls God the only Sovereign and the King of kings and Lord of lords, a compact New Testament royal-master formulation beside Mālik.

basis: Everyone appears before Christ's judgment seat
note: The commentary joins malik with the Day of Judgment; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive what is due, adding personal accountability to the sovereign judgment motif.

basis: all appear before Christ's judgment seat
note: All people must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds, an individual accounting scene for the Day of dīn dimension.

basis: Cornelius falls at a human's feet
note: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet and prostrates before him, staging the very transfer of honor to a human figure that the commentary's limit on human lords excludes.

basis: Peter refuses human prostration
note: Peter raises Cornelius and says that he too is human, turning the preceding act into an explicit rejection of worshipful elevation of a person.

basis: Human beings refuse worship and point to the Creator
note: The commentary calls God the one worshipped and treats humans as created servants; Paul and Barnabas reject a crowd's worship, identify themselves as human, and direct it to the living Creator, clarifying why a human must not take divine honor.

basis: God made the world and is Lord of heaven and earth
note: Paul calls the creator Lord of heaven and earth, a New Testament statement of comprehensive divine sovereignty over the worlds named in the commentary.

basis: The Creator gives life and is not served from need
note: The commentary grounds human service in being created and treats God as owner; Paul says the world's maker is not served by human hands as though needy, because he gives life and all things, distinguishing worship from supplying a master's lack.

basis: God is not served as needing anything
note: God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, because he gives life and breath to all; it closely supports the commentary's insistence that the true owner lacks no helper and is not reduced by need.

basis: a fixed day for judging the world
note: Paul says God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, making the day-and-judgment element explicit in the same speech that calls God creator and Lord.

basis: direct prayer to creator as Sovereign Master
note: The community addresses God as despota, the Sovereign Master who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; it joins direct address, mastery, and creation in one prayer.

basis: slaves serve the Lord Christ
note: In an instruction to household slaves, Paul says that the service ultimately rendered is to the Lord Christ and promises an inheritance, placing earthly service under a different master and reward.

basis: Earthly masters have a Master in heaven
note: The commentary links a human owner to the higher owner who rules all; Paul tells masters to act justly because they too have a Master in heaven, limiting household power under divine authority.

basis: earthly masters share a Master in heaven
note: Christian masters must stop threatening because their own and their slaves' Master is in heaven and shows no partiality; the verse limits human ownership from above.

basis: no longer slave but child and heir
note: The believer is no longer a slave but a child and heir through God, changing the household relation from permanent servitude to filial inheritance.

basis: make straight paths for feet
note: Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than put out of joint, turning the made-level road into a communal moral action.

basis: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
note: The community is to offer acceptable worship to God with reverence and awe because it receives an unshakable kingdom, a liturgical form of humble service before sovereignty.

basis: Moses faithful as a servant in God's house
note: The commentary pictures a human servant in the owner's house; Hebrews calls Moses faithful as a servant within God's house, placing the Mosaic figure in a divine household and clarifying the servant's subordinate role.

basis: Moses as servant in God's whole house
note: Moses is faithful as a servant in all God's house, preserving the commentary's house/master/servant relation in an explicitly theological household.

basis: The Son stands over the house
note: The commentary distinguishes the owner from the servant who belongs in the owner's house; Hebrews contrasts Moses the servant with Christ as Son over God's house, making household status the basis of a theological distinction.

basis: Christ as Son over God's house
note: The contrast makes Christ Son over God's house and the believers that house, distinguishing sonship and household membership from slave status.

basis: all animal kinds are tamed
note: James says every kind of beast, bird, reptile, and sea creature is tamed by humanity, a precise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's language of animal domestication.

basis: the tongue cannot be tamed
note: The immediately following contrast says no human can tame the tongue; it gives the tamed-animal figure a moral reversal in which the human speaker remains resistant to mastery.

basis: One lawgiver and judge can save or destroy
note: The commentary says God alone is the owner and judge while humans must not make one another lords; James names one lawgiver and judge able to save and destroy, explicitly grounding the limit on judging others in God's singular authority.

basis: Aramaic/Hebrew rabbî as a teacher's title
note: The commentary's source label ر ب ب explains rabb as an obeyed master and human household owner; John's disciples address Jesus as Rabbi and the Gospel glosses the title as Teacher, showing the Semitic cognate in a teacher-authority setting.

basis: “Teacher and Lord”
note: Jesus accepts the disciples' titles “Teacher” and “Lord,” giving the human speech of lordship in the commentary an explicit Gospel parallel before the following reversal.

basis: The Lord and Teacher washes his disciples' feet
note: The commentary distinguishes the owner from the humiliated servant; Jesus explicitly takes the role of teacher and Lord while washing his disciples' feet, making a servant's lowly work the action of the master.

basis: Lord washes servants' feet
note: The one called Lord and Teacher washes disciples' feet and makes it exemplary; the action directly counters the commentary's asymmetry in which humiliation belongs only to the servant.

basis: A servant is not greater than the master
note: The commentary's image depends on the servant's subordination to the owner; Jesus uses the servant/master relation to set the disciples' status after washing their feet, while the scene has already shown the master serving.

basis: Disciples no longer called slaves but friends
note: The commentary presents the human as God's owned servant by creation; Jesus says his disciples are no longer slaves who lack knowledge of the master's affairs but friends who have been told what he heard, adding a Christian shift from subordination to disclosed intimacy.

basis: no longer servants but friends
note: Jesus no longer calls disciples servants because a servant does not know the master's affairs, but friends; intimate disclosure revises the distance assumed by the master-property model.

basis: slave and son in the household
note: Jesus says a slave does not remain in the household forever but the son does; it uses the house image to contrast slave impermanence with filial permanence.

basis: master serves watchful servants
note: The returning master dresses for service, seats his servants, and serves them; this deliberately reverses the commentary's one-way household hierarchy and its claim that the master does not lower himself.

basis: returning son asks to be a hired servant
note: The returning son proposes admission to his father's house as a hired servant; paired with the father's response in verse 22, it makes the commentary's servant-at-the-master's-house image a precise Gospel encounter.

basis: father restores the returning son with honor
note: The father answers the returning son's household shame with robe, ring, and sandals, making the master's house a place of restorative honor rather than the fixed abasement expected in the commentary.

basis: Servants say they have done their duty
note: The commentary's speaker says in the first-person plural that they worship and explains worship as obedient submission; Jesus has servants conclude that they have only done their duty, giving a concrete household form for service without claiming merit.

basis: servants have done only their duty
note: After doing all commanded, disciples are to call themselves servants who have only done their duty; it supplies a Christian idiom of obedience and lowly self-description.

basis: servant returns from plowing or shepherding
note: Jesus' household example assumes a servant who comes in from field work and still prepares the master's meal, preserving the literal labor-and-master scene that underlies the commentary's slave image.

basis: leveling and smoothing the way
note: Luke's Isaian quotation retains valleys filled, mountains lowered, and rough places made smooth; it carries the commentary's rendered-road image into the Gospel's preparation for God's coming.

basis: calling Lord requires obedience
note: Jesus asks why people call him “Lord, Lord” but do not do what he says; the verse explicitly joins the master's title to obedience, not to verbal address alone.

basis: prepare the Lord's way, make paths straight
note: Mark applies the wilderness-road summons to John's proclamation, making the straightened path a concrete Gospel preparation for the Lord rather than a bare travel image.

basis: Gentile rulers lord it over others
note: Jesus names dominating rule as the practice of Gentile rulers, making human lordship a social pattern that his teaching will explicitly reject.

basis: greatness becomes service
note: The next verse reverses status: whoever wants greatness must become the others' servant, changing the master-slave scale from ownership to service.

basis: Son of Man serves and gives ransom
note: The Son of Man comes not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom, a concentrated counter-scene to a master who only receives service.

basis: A king settles accounts with servants
note: The commentary joins Malik and Dīn as sovereign and judgment; Jesus begins a parable with a king settling accounts with his servants, giving a household scene in which ownership and reckoning meet.

basis: A debtor and his household sold into slavery
note: The commentary links Dīn to subduing, enslavement, and possession; in the king's reckoning a debtor is ordered sold with his family and possessions, concretely combining debt judgment with human ownership.

basis: servant falls before master over debt
note: The servant falls down before his master and begs for patience over the debt, giving a literal scene of servile prostration, ownership, and reckoning.

basis: master releases servant and forgives debt
note: The master is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and cancels the debt; this masterly authority is expressed through liberation rather than permanent subjection.

basis: Greatness as becoming a slave
note: The commentary calls worship the servant's utmost humbling and warns against humans making one another lords; Jesus says the first must become the others' slave, reversing status within a human hierarchy.

basis: The Son of Man serves rather than receives service
note: The commentary presents the master as owner and the servant as the one humbled; Jesus describes the Son of Man as serving and giving his life, placing service in the role of the exalted figure.

basis: gentle king mounted on donkey
note: Matthew presents the king as gentle and mounted on a donkey, carrying Zechariah's master-humility-and-domesticated-animal figure into the Gospel entry scene.

basis: Rabbi title and shared brotherhood
note: The commentary warns against taking one another as lords; Jesus tells disciples not to seek the title Rabbi because they are brothers and have one teacher, a specific Christian limit on human religious authority.

basis: master entrusts property to servants
note: The parable begins with a man entrusting his own property to his servants, preserving the master-property-servant relation that the commentary treats as a single image.

basis: master returns to settle accounts
note: The servants' master returns after a long time and settles accounts with them, a literal parabolic meeting of ownership, service, and the reckoning associated with the Day of dīn.

basis: The King sits in judgment
note: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; Jesus depicts the Son of Man coming in glory and sitting on a throne, giving the judgment scene an enthroned sovereign.

basis: Nations gathered and separated for judgment
note: The commentary's Day of Judgment includes a sovereign who rules over servants; Jesus gathers all nations before the enthroned figure and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep, adding a universal judgment scene.

basis: The judge names himself King and assigns inheritance
note: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; after nations are gathered and separated, the figure calls himself King and assigns an inheritance, locating kingship in his verdict.

basis: Worship and serve God alone
note: The commentary's 1:5 makes worship exclusive and defines it through obedient submission; Jesus answers the tempter by directing worship and service to God alone, pairing the two acts in a concrete temptation scene.

basis: worship and serve God alone
note: Jesus answers temptation with worship of and service to God alone, a direct Gospel formulation of the exclusive “you we worship” relation.

basis: One slave cannot serve two masters
note: The commentary's servant speaks allegiance to one owner; Jesus says a slave cannot serve two masters and contrasts God with wealth, making divided ownership the practical test of exclusive devotion.

basis: no one can serve two masters
note: The maxim about serving God or Mammon makes divided mastership impossible, a close counterpart to the commentary's restriction on treating people or possessions as rival lords.

basis: Isaiah's universal bowing applied to Jesus
note: The commentary says every human belongs to God by creation; Philippians reuses Isaiah's universal knee-bowing image for Jesus, giving the earlier monotheistic passage a specifically Christological reading.

basis: every knee bends at Jesus' name
note: The universal bending of knees echoes the commentary's eschatological servanthood, but directs it in the hymn's Christological pattern.

basis: Universal confession that Jesus is Lord
note: The commentary says worship belongs to the divine owner; Philippians applies Isaiah's universal confession to Jesus as Lord, a Christian interpretation that identifies the honored figure in the universal submission scene.

basis: every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
note: The final confession calls Jesus “Lord” to the Father's glory, pairing the master's title, universal confession, and worship after the servant-form reversal.

basis: Christ in God's form
note: The hymn begins with Christ in God's form, establishing the high status whose subsequent self-emptying makes its relation to the commentary's unlowered owner deliberate rather than generic humility.

basis: The Lord takes a slave's form
note: The commentary locates humiliation in the servant and says the owner does not undergo humiliation; the Christian hymn says Christ takes a slave's form, a striking reversal in which the one confessed as Lord assumes the servant's station.

basis: form of a slave
note: Christ takes the form of a slave; the verse turns the commentary's owned and humbled slave role into the role voluntarily assumed by the exalted figure.

basis: The servant-form is expressed as humility and obedience
note: The commentary defines worship as the utmost humbling and links the servant with obedience; the hymn describes Christ humbling himself and becoming obedient to death, while assigning this path to the exalted figure.

basis: humbled obedience to death
note: The hymn explicitly says he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, matching the commentary's association of worship/service with abasement while reversing who undergoes it.

basis: God highly exalts the humbled one
note: God's exaltation follows the slave-form and humbling, giving the commentary's secondary movement from lowliness to honor a markedly different Christian sequence.

basis: no longer a slave but a beloved brother
note: Paul asks that Onesimus be received no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother in the Lord, an explicit Christian re-description of an owned person's relation.

basis: fear, glory, judgment, worship the creator
note: The angel announces judgment and commands worship of the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs, bringing creator-ownership and Day-of-judgment worship together.

basis: fellow servant; worship God
note: The angel refuses John's prostration, identifies as a fellow servant, and commands worship of God; it sharply distinguishes servanthood from receiving worship.

basis: all God's servants praise him
note: A heavenly voice calls all God's servants, great and small, to praise him; it provides a direct apocalyptic equivalent to praise voiced by those who belong to God.

basis: The dead judged before the throne
note: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; Revelation's throne scene opens books and judges the dead according to their deeds, a direct eschatological counterpart.

basis: God's servants worship at the throne
note: The commentary calls the servant the owned person who worships God; Revelation's final vision says God's servants worship him at his throne, joining servant identity, worship, and the divine household.

basis: God's servants serve in the final city
note: In the city of God's throne and the Lamb's throne, the servants will serve him; the final setting gives an eschatological counterpart to universal divine service.

basis: Servants see God's face
note: The commentary pictures the slave as belonging to the owner's house; Revelation promises God's servants access to his face and name, adding intimate presence to the household relation.

basis: Creation exists by God's will and worships him
note: The commentary grounds universal servitude in God's act of creating; heaven's worship in Revelation calls God creator of all things and says they exist by his will, directly linking creation and divine honor.

basis: direct praise to the creator
note: The heavenly elders say directly, “You are worthy,” because God created all things by his will; it closely joins praise, direct address, and creation-based sovereignty.

basis: Every creature worships the throne and the Lamb
note: The commentary says all who are created come as servants to God; Revelation gives praise from every creature to the throne and the Lamb, extending the universal service image while including the Lamb alongside God.

basis: Sovereign Lord asked to judge
note: The martyrs address God as Sovereign Lord and ask when God will judge, bringing master-language and the delayed final judgment into a single direct prayer.

basis: bodies offered as living sacrifice and worship
note: Paul calls the presentation of embodied life to God a living sacrifice and rational worship, giving worship a concrete, whole-person form beyond a merely verbal confession.

basis: another person's household servant
note: A believer is called another's household servant who stands or falls before his own Lord; the verse makes mastership a reason not to usurp judgment over someone else's servant.

basis: Obedience makes one a slave
note: The commentary links Dīn with obedience and the slave with being humbled; Paul says people become slaves to the one they obey, directly joining obedience to servile status.

basis: slaves of the one obeyed
note: Paul states that a person becomes a slave of the one obeyed, whether sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness; it closely binds slavery to obedience as the commentary's dīn discussion does.

basis: Freed from sin and enslaved to God
note: The commentary says both free and enslaved humans are God's servants by creation; Paul describes people freed from sin and enslaved to God, a specific transformation of status that makes the paradox explicit.

basis: freed from sin, enslaved to God
note: Paul calls believers both freed from sin and enslaved to God, a consciously paradoxical account of divine belonging and moral freedom.

basis: not slavery to fear but adoption
note: Paul contrasts a spirit of slavery leading to fear with adoption that cries “Abba, Father,” offering a different mode of direct address and belonging from the commentary's servile abasement.

basis: The Elect One enthroned to judge sinners
note: The commentary joins Malik with the Day of Judgment; Enoch seats the Elect One on a throne of glory and describes the destruction of sinners before him, an apocalyptic expansion of enthroned authority as judicial rule.

basis: Earthly kings fall before the enthroned Son of Man
note: The commentary links sovereign rule to the humiliation of servants before their owner; Enoch depicts kings and powerful people falling before the enthroned Son of Man and seeking mercy, extending the image of universal subordination into Jewish apocalyptic judgment.

basis: prepare the way through Torah study
note: The Community Rule applies Isaiah's wilderness-way language to a separated group preparing God's way by studying and doing Torah, an interpretive conversion of road-making into disciplined obedience.

basis: The pierced ear recalls that Israel belongs to God
note: The commentary says the servant is God's by creation and describes human beings as enslaved by other people; this rabbinic interpretation of the permanent Hebrew slave's pierced ear says the ear heard that Israel belongs to God and should not become a slave to slaves, directly limiting human ownership.

basis: level ground for Israel's safe walking
note: Baruch says God commands mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel may walk safely on level ground, a Jewish expansion of Isaiah's road image into divinely prepared passage.

basis: servants serving without reward
note: Antigonus instructs disciples to serve the master without serving for reward and to keep the fear of heaven; it probes how divine service can be freely offered rather than merely compelled.

basis: yoke of Torah releases other yokes
note: The mishnah says accepting the yoke of Torah removes the yoke of government and worldly burdens; it develops divine submission as release from rival subjections.

basis: yoke of heaven and commandments
note: Rabbi Joshua ben Korha explains the order of the Shema as first accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven and then the yoke of commandments; this gives a Jewish liturgical reading of willingly assumed divine obedience.

basis: Serving God without seeking a reward
note: The commentary stresses worship as a servant's status and obedience, not merely a feeling; Antigonus teaches that servants should serve their master without serving for a reward, adding a motive-focused Jewish reading of divine service.

basis: Reciting Shema as accepting heaven's yoke
note: The commentary reads 1:5 as a spoken acceptance of belonging and obedience to God; this rabbinic ordering says Shema first accepts the yoke of heaven and then the commandments, giving liturgical interpretation to the servant's first-person pledge.

basis: Donkey's burden and the slave's work
note: The commentary moves from a camel subdued by tar to a humbled human slave; Sirach places fodder, stick, and burden for a donkey beside bread, discipline, and work for a slave, explicitly bringing animal control and human servitude together.

basis: donkey's burden and slave's work
note: Greek Sirach pairs fodder, stick, and burdens for a donkey with bread, discipline, and work for a slave, explicitly yoking animal taming and human subjection as the commentary does.

basis: A master assigns a servant work and finds rest
note: The commentary describes a human owner using a slave's labor and calls the servant humbled by work; Sirach says setting the servant to work gives the master rest, making the labor relation explicit.

basis: Yoke and harness bend a servant's neck
note: The commentary's common image is one who has been subdued; Sirach describes yoke and harness bending the neck and punishment for a bad servant, offering a concrete Jewish parallel for bodily subjection.

basis: Work imposed to prevent idleness
note: The commentary explains the slave through work that lowers him; Sirach commands work for the servant and treats idleness as a danger, adding an ancient household ethic to the labor image.

basis: servant treated as brother
note: After its donkey-and-slave discipline imagery, Sirach tells the owner to treat a servant as a brother; the nearby ethical reversal complicates a reading of the owned person as only property.

basis: all comes from God; gifts returned
note: David's praise says all things come from God and that Israel gives only what is already God's; it makes praise an acknowledgment that human possessions remain received goods.

basis: Israel challenged to choose whom to follow
note: The commentary hears a first-person commitment to worship one alone; Elijah confronts Israel's divided allegiance between the Lord and Baal, placing exclusive service in a public contest over rival gods.

basis: Exiles refuse royal demand to worship an image
note: The commentary's 1:5 makes worship exclusive despite human power; the Judeans refuse the king's command to worship his image, showing allegiance to God under an imperial test.

basis: refusal to serve gods or worship the image
note: The Judean servants tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his golden image, a concrete refusal of a ruler's imposed cultic mastery.

basis: Aramaic דינא for judgment
note: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن and links it to humbling, enslavement, possession, and the Day of Judgment; Daniel's Aramaic cognate root names the court's judgment, directly matching the judgment sense while not supporting those other senses.

basis: Arabic د ي ن (source labels B001, B004), Aramaic דינא
note: Daniel's Aramaic heavenly court says that the dīn sat and books were opened; the cognate juridical word keeps the judgment sense of “Day of dīn” beside the commentary's developed obedience and ownership senses.

basis: Dominion and service of the humanlike figure
note: The commentary joins malik sovereignty to the servant's worship; Daniel gives everlasting dominion to one like a son of man and says peoples and languages will serve him, a close image of universal service under a ruler with a distinct figure in the vision.

basis: Release of a servant grounded in Israel's own slavery
note: The commentary develops the human owner and enslaved person's status; Deuteronomy requires a master to release a Hebrew servant generously because Israel remembers being enslaved in Egypt and redeemed by God, adding an ethical consequence to divine ownership.

basis: Hebrew דִּין for judging his people and servants
note: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن and connects it to both the Day of Judgment and the servant's subjection; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew root for the Lord judging his people and showing compassion to his servants, pairing judgment with the servant relation.

basis: Father who made and acquired you
note: The song calls God the Father who made, acquired, and established Israel, closely matching the commentary's claim that createdness establishes a prior divine belonging.

basis: servant rests “as you do”
note: The Decalogue's Sabbath law requires the male and female servant to rest as the owner rests; it turns the master-slave relation into an equality of rest before God.

basis: Hebrew עבד for exclusive service
note: The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for worship and service and reads 1:5 as service to God alone; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד in its command to serve the Lord alone, giving a direct lexical and ethical counterpart.

basis: Arabic إله/الله (source label ء ل ه B001), Hebrew אלהיך
note: The command to fear and serve “YHWH your God” uses Hebrew אלהיך from the same ʾ-l-h family as the commentary's ilāh/Allah label and directs exclusive service toward that God.

basis: God brings every deed into judgment
note: The closing maxim says God will bring every deed, hidden or open, into judgment, providing an explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the reckoning implied by Day of dīn.

basis: Pharaoh's forced labor of Israel
note: The commentary's Moses scene contrasts being raised in Pharaoh's house with Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; Exodus describes the same people forced into labor, giving the human domination behind that contrast.

basis: Arabic ع ب د (source labels B001-B006), Hebrew עבד
note: Egyptians force Israelites into harsh service; the Hebrew verb is from עבד, a genuine cognate of the commentary's Arabic ع ب د, and its context preserves the coerced labor side of the root.

basis: Harsh labor and servitude in Egypt
note: The commentary's account of Pharaoh enslaving Israel is matched by Exodus's description of bitter labor under Egyptian taskmasters; the narrative adds the grinding work through which human rule humbles its subjects.

basis: Israel released from serving Egypt
note: When Israel has gone, Egypt describes the loss as letting them go “from serving us”; the phrasing gives the Pharaoh-Israel bondage in the commentary a direct narrative counterpart.

basis: Moses raised in Pharaoh's household
note: The commentary pairs Pharaoh's claim to have raised Moses with his enslavement of Israel; Exodus says Pharaoh's daughter raises Moses as her son in the palace, preserving the family-raising detail while locating it specifically with the daughter.

basis: house, servants, ox, donkey, every possession
note: The anti-coveting command gathers a neighbor's house, male and female servants, ox, donkey, and other possessions into one household inventory, closely matching the commentary's owner-house-animal-slave tableau.

basis: The Lord identifies himself as Israel's redeemer from slavery
note: The commentary grounds human belonging to God in creation and contrasts divine ownership with Pharaoh's human enslavement; the covenant begins by naming the Lord who brought Israel out of a slave-house, making exclusive allegiance a response to liberation.

basis: No bowing to or serving other gods
note: The commentary reads 1:5 as exclusive worship of the one owner; this command prohibits bowing to other gods and serving them, specifying the covenantal acts excluded by that allegiance.

basis: Arabic ع ب د (source labels B001-B006), Hebrew עבד
note: The prohibition against bowing to or serving other gods uses Hebrew עבד; it gives the cognate root an explicit exclusive-worship setting rather than merely a lexical resemblance.

basis: A Hebrew servant leaves after six years
note: The commentary describes humans as God's servants by creation, not by an initial choice; this law limits a human master's claim to six years and requires release in the seventh, distinguishing temporary human servitude from the creator's prior claim.

basis: slave described as master's money
note: The assault law calls the slave the master's “money”; it directly witnesses the property vocabulary that the commentary places inside the master-slave relation.

basis: A slave chooses to remain with his master
note: The commentary says human servitude to God begins through creation rather than a slave's choice; this law has a Hebrew slave declare love for his master and refuse release, a concrete human bond chosen after the term of service.

basis: servant chooses master, wife, children, household
note: The Hebrew servant says that he loves his master, wife, and children and will not go free; this gives a legal counter-case in which continued belonging is explicitly voiced as a choice.

basis: doorpost, pierced ear, permanent service
note: The master brings the willing servant to the doorpost and pierces his ear for lifelong service, a concrete ritualization of ownership and enduring service in the master's house.

basis: Sabbath rest for ox, donkey, servant
note: The Sabbath command joins the ox and donkey to the child of the slave woman and resident alien in receiving rest, placing a divine limit on the labor imposed upon both working animals and dependent people.

basis: Israel released to serve God
note: The commentary contrasts human enslavement with worship due to God; here God demands that Pharaoh release Israel so the people can serve God, recasting the exodus as a transfer from Pharaoh's forced labor to divine service.

basis: Hebrew עבד for service to God
note: The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for both worship and human enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד for Israel's service to God, showing the cultic use of the same Semitic service word in the story of release from forced labor.

basis: release my son to serve me
note: God tells Pharaoh to release Israel, called God's son, “that he may serve me”; Hebrew תעבדני shares the ʿbd root with naʿbudu and turns release from Pharaoh into service of God.

basis: Every life belongs to God in a judgment context
note: The commentary joins God's malik status to human servitude; Ezekiel declares every life God's and then speaks of individual accountability, connecting divine ownership with judgment rather than human possession.

basis: all lives are God's
note: God declares that every life, parent and child alike, is God's; the assertion broadens the commentary's ownership image from a household slave to all human persons.

basis: human dominion over living creatures
note: The creation command tells humankind to subdue the earth and rule the animals, providing a creation account of the animal authority and use developed through the tamed camel and livestock.

basis: enslaved people and divine judgment
note: God says that the nation whom Abraham's descendants serve will be judged; it joins Israel's forced service to judgment, the two poles carried by the commentary's slave language and Day of dīn.

basis: master, servant, camels, goods in hand
note: Abraham's servant takes his master's camels, with “all the good things of his master” in his hand; the verse supplies a concrete owner-animal-servant tableau for the commentary's property and domestication image.

basis: a servant speaks for his master
note: The speaker identifies himself as Abraham's servant, a close narrative counterpart to the owned person speaking in the first person after the commentary's shift to “we worship you.”

basis: master's livestock, servants, camels, donkeys
note: The servant lists his master's wealth as animals, male and female servants, and camels and donkeys, making the commentary's linked possessions socially concrete.

basis: Joseph serves Potiphar and is set over his household
note: The commentary uses Yusuf's human rabb as an owner who gives him a good home; Genesis places Joseph as servant in Potiphar's house and then makes him its manager, supplying the matching household relation in the shared Joseph story.

basis: Joseph, Egyptian master, house, all in hand
note: Joseph serves the Egyptian official, is set over his house, and receives everything the master owns into his hand; this is the biblical Joseph-household setting behind the commentary's human rab/master scene.

basis: Joseph's master leaves his house and possessions in Joseph's hand
note: The commentary describes rabb as owner of a house and malik as what a hand possesses; Genesis gives Joseph authority over his master's house while Potiphar retains ownership, sharpening the distinction between a human master's trust and ownership.

basis: master's wife commands Joseph
note: The Egyptian master's wife orders Joseph to lie with her, the immediate biblical scene corresponding to the commentary's Joseph speaking to the woman in his Egyptian master's house.

basis: my master, house, withheld possession
note: Joseph calls the Egyptian “my master” and describes his control over the house and its goods, giving a precise human-master use alongside the commentary's discussion of rabbi as an owner.

basis: human master bounded by sin against God
note: Joseph says his master has withheld nothing but his wife, yet refuses because the act would be a sin against God; the human householder's wide control is subordinated to a higher Lord.

basis: animals placed into human hand
note: After the flood, every animal is given into human hands; the phrase makes ownership/control of creatures a concrete parallel to the commentary's hand-held property and subdued animals.

basis: trained heifer, fair neck, yoke
note: Hosea depicts Ephraim as a trained heifer whose neck will be yoked for plowing, a close animal image for the commentary's domestication, submission, and forced labor.

basis: ox knows owner, donkey its master's manger
note: The ox recognizes its owner and the donkey its master's feeding-place, while Israel does not know; animal ownership becomes a rebuke about recognizing and obeying the divine master.

basis: judge, lawgiver, king
note: YHWH is named Israel's judge, lawgiver, and king; the verse gathers the judicial and sovereign dimensions that meet in the commentary's Mālik of the Day of dīn.

basis: A road prepared in the wilderness
note: The commentary's road is made passable by being trampled and subdued; Isaiah calls for a way prepared in the wilderness, a specific road-making image that may illuminate the comparison, though the Hebrew passage does not use the commentary's Arabic root.

basis: prepare and straighten God's highway
note: The wilderness voice commands a way to be prepared and a highway made straight for God, the nearest biblical counterpart to the commentary's trodden, made-level road.

basis: Uneven ground leveled for a road
note: The commentary glosses the road as flattened and made traversable; Isaiah describes valleys raised and mountains lowered as the route is made level, an adjacent but distinct image of making a road passable.

basis: valleys raised, mountains lowered, rough ground level
note: The next verse specifies the leveling and smoothing of the road, adding the physical process of subduing terrain rather than only the abstract image of a path.

basis: Israel formed by God and called his own
note: The commentary says the human servant belongs to God by being created; Isaiah addresses Jacob as formed by God and says he is God's, joining creation, personal address, and possession in one promise.

basis: created, formed, redeemed, “you are mine”
note: The creator-former addresses Israel by name and says “you are mine,” an unusually direct biblical formulation of created persons as belonging to God.

basis: formed servant
note: Israel is told, “you are my servant; I formed you,” joining servanthood to divine formation in the same sequence the commentary makes explicit.

basis: Every knee bends and every tongue swears
note: The commentary says every human is already God's servant by creation and that the servant addresses God directly; Isaiah pictures universal bodily submission and confession before God, adding a public, eschatological form of that allegiance.

basis: every knee bows to God
note: God's oath that every knee will bend before him gives a universal biblical scene of bodily submission corresponding to the commentary's claim that all creatures finally come as servants.

basis: exalted servant
note: God's servant is described as raised, lifted up, and greatly exalted, supplying a scriptural servant-and-honor trajectory beside the commentary's muʿabbad sense.

basis: fasting that breaks every yoke
note: The fast God chooses loosens bonds, frees the oppressed, and breaks every yoke; it makes worship answer human subjugation by liberation rather than by extending it.

basis: Arabic م ل ك (source label B002), Hebrew מלך
note: Isaiah sees YHWH as “the King”; Hebrew מלך shares the m-l-k root with the commentary's Mālik label, while the verse contributes royal sovereignty rather than treating the Hebrew word as a property term.

basis: Father, potter, clay, work of hands
note: The prayer calls God Father and potter and the people clay made by God's hand, a creation-and-forming image for dependence that does not reduce them to household property.

basis: clay in potter's hand, house of Israel
note: God compares the house of Israel to clay in a potter's hand, a particularly close biblical image for formed material held under a maker's authority.

basis: life of animals and humans in God's hand
note: Job places the life of every living creature and the breath of all humanity in God's hand, extending the commentary's hand-held possession figure beyond livestock to all life.

basis: one creator of master and servant
note: Job grounds a servant's right to a hearing in the fact that the same maker formed both master and servant in the womb; it answers creation-based ownership with creation-based equality.

basis: wild ox refuses service and manger
note: God asks whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or lodge by the manger; its refusal marks the limit of human animal mastery that the commentary depicts as divinely granted.

basis: everything under heaven belongs to God
note: God asks who could give first so that God owed repayment, because all under heaven is God's; it joins universal possession to divine non-dependence.

basis: choose whom to serve; household service
note: Joshua makes service a confessed choice—“as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH”—which closely parallels the commentary's movement from an existing status to the servant's own voiced assent.

basis: Collective pledge to serve and obey the Lord
note: The commentary hears the owned servant speak directly to the owner in the first-person plural; Israel here answers in a collective pledge to serve the Lord and obey his voice, adding a covenantal setting for that spoken allegiance.

basis: Israelites are God's servants and not human property
note: The commentary says all people belong to God whether free or enslaved; Leviticus grounds Israel's status as God's servants in the exodus and bars their sale as slaves, limiting human ownership by God's prior claim.

basis: Israel belongs to God, not sale as slaves
note: Because Israelites are God's servants brought from Egypt, they may not be sold in a slave sale; it qualifies the owner-slave analogy by denying an Israelite human master an absolute claim.

basis: do not rule ruthlessly over a servant
note: The law prohibits ruthless rule over an impoverished Israelite servant and requires fear of God, placing a divine limit on the domination developed in the commentary.

basis: slaves as inherited possession
note: The law permits inherited, permanent possession of foreign slaves, a stark legal counterpart to the commentary's technical treatment of a mamlūk as property.

basis: “My servants” and deliverance from Egypt
note: God twice calls Israelites “my servants”; the verse makes divine ownership the reason they are not ultimately servants of human owners.

basis: servant honors master, God as master
note: Malachi argues from a servant's honor for a master to God's claim on Israel's honor, directly using household hierarchy to define proper reverence for God.

basis: wise servant shares a son's inheritance
note: A prudent servant rules over a shameful son and shares the inheritance with the brothers, overturning a fixed hierarchy of owner, household, and slave.

basis: one guarding a master is honored
note: Proverbs says the one who keeps or attends to a master will be honored, a compact wisdom parallel to the commentary's secondary possibility that service and honor meet.

basis: serve God with gladness
note: The liturgical command to serve YHWH joyfully gives a cultic form of service that is more than inward feeling, while changing the commentary's stress on extreme abasement.

basis: made by God, his people and flock
note: WLC's ketiv reads that God made us “and not we [ourselves],” while its qere reads “and we are his”; the verse then calls the people his and the flock of his pasture, so both streams need to be kept distinct in this creation-and-belonging parallel.

basis: Creation, belonging, and the ketiv/qere
note: The commentary grounds universal servitude in being created; this verse names God as maker and Israel as his people and pasture's flock. WLC's ketiv reads ולא אנחנו, while the qere reads ולו אנחנו, so explicit wording that the people are God's belongs to the qere.

basis: The worshipper calls himself God's servant and recalls released bonds
note: The commentary makes the servant speak directly to the owner; the psalmist calls himself the Lord's servant and says God has loosed his bonds, adding a first-person prayer of servitude after deliverance.

basis: direct “I am your servant”; bonds loosed
note: The psalmist directly calls himself God's servant and son of God's maidservant, then says God has loosed his bonds; it keeps divine servanthood and liberation together in one prayer.

basis: All creation as God's servants
note: The commentary says people are God's servants by being brought into existence; the psalm says the created order stands by God's ordinances and calls all things his servants, extending the service image beyond humanity.

basis: servants' eyes to master's hand
note: The psalm compares Israel's eyes toward God to servants' eyes toward a master's hand and a maid's toward her mistress; it is an exact prayer-image of dependent, direct address.

basis: Servants watch their masters' hands
note: The commentary describes the owned servant's posture before a master; the psalm compares worshippers' gaze toward God to the eyes of male and female servants fixed on their masters' hands, giving a precise domestic image for dependence in prayer.

basis: third-person shepherd narration turns to “you”
note: Psalm 23 moves from “he” as the shepherd who leads in verses 1-3 to direct “you” in verse 4; its exact pronoun turn offers a literary analogue to the commentary's movement from third-person praise to second-person address, though its figure is shepherd and flock.

basis: The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
note: The commentary's malik image includes everything held in the owner's hand; this psalm assigns the earth and all within it to the Lord, extending the property image from household goods to the world.

basis: earth and inhabitants belong to YHWH
note: The psalm's opening ownership formula gives YHWH the earth, its fullness, the world, and its inhabitants, an explicit scriptural horizon for “Lord of the worlds.”

basis: Bit and bridle restrain horse and mule
note: The commentary's B005 gloss makes a subdued camel an image of submission; this proverb says an uncomprehending person must be restrained like a horse or mule with bit and bridle, while using the image as a warning against stubbornness rather than praising domination.

basis: cattle belong to God
note: God claims every forest animal and the cattle on a thousand hills; human possession of livestock is set within the creator's prior ownership.

basis: Humans given rule over livestock
note: The commentary opens with an owner of animals and then says humans themselves are God's servants by creation; the psalm places sheep, cattle, and wild animals under human rule, showing delegated animal mastery beneath divine creation.

basis: Bowing and kneeling before the maker
note: The commentary calls worship the utmost humbling of the servant; the psalm invites worshippers to bow and kneel before their maker, giving bodily posture to its account of submission.

basis: bow, kneel, maker
note: The congregation is summoned to bow down and kneel before YHWH its maker, a close liturgical image of embodied abasement before the creator.

basis: People as sheep of God's hand
note: The commentary makes the servant God's owned person and places him in the master's house; the psalm calls the worshippers God's people and the sheep of his hand, combining belonging with a shepherd's care.

basis: people of pasture, flock of God's hand
note: The worshippers are God's people and the flock of his hand; it combines animal dependence, the owner's hand, and collective divine belonging.

basis: Hebrew מלך for kingship
note: The commentary labels Arabic م ل ك for malik as owner and sovereign; Zechariah uses the cognate Hebrew מלך for the Lord's kingship over the whole earth, showing the sovereign sense without importing the commentary's separate property sense.

basis: humble king riding a donkey
note: Zion's king comes righteous and victorious yet humble, mounted on a donkey; the royal figure unites authority, lowliness, and a domesticated animal in a configuration that reverses the commentary's unlowered master.

basis: Creation serves its maker
note: The commentary says all humans come to God as servants because he created them; Wisdom says creation itself serves its maker, extending the creator-servant relation from humanity to the natural order.

basis: acquiring a Hebrew servant acquires a master
note: The Talmud's maxim that one who acquires a Hebrew servant acquires a master develops Torah's service law into a reversal: the owner must meet the servant's needs so fully that mastery is ethically displaced.

basis: ear piercing and servants of God
note: The Talmud explains the permanently pierced Hebrew servant through the Sinai claim that Israel belongs to God, criticizing one who acquires a human master; it is a direct Jewish limit on human lordship.
